slides.h: If our universe sits inside a black hole, should the sky look lopsided?
b: One published model puts a shock-wave wall around everything we can see. If we are not at the exact center, the sky should differ toward the wall.
Does what we actually observe rule that out?

slides.h: Inside the wall, the sky is exactly normal — from anywhere
b: The expansion looks identical in every direction no matter how far off center you stand. Not slightly lopsided: exactly zero.
That killed our own starting idea — a lopsided expansion rate was supposed to be the giveaway.

slides.h: One round patch of altered sky, in one direction
b: If the wall is close enough that the oldest light reaches past it, we would see a patch tens of degrees wide around one axis. Nothing else.
The hiding rule: under about 20 percent off center, every ray stays inside and the wall is invisible.

slides.h: 18 frozen measurements — and the shapes do not match
b: Each quote checked against its own source, both sides of two unsettled arguments carried.
All 7 large-angle measurements are statistics of the whole sky at once. The fingerprint is a bounded patch.

slides.h: Not ruled out, not supported — the evidence is the wrong shape
b: On the 4 criteria written in advance: localization fails on all 7 rows, patch character fails on all 7, and the angular-size evidence is an honest gap.
What is new: a quantified hiding condition, and one named way to make it testable — compute what light crossing the wall looks like.

slides.h: The criteria were locked before the comparison
b: The brief has not changed since registration — verified byte for byte by the reviewing engine.
When our execution bent one criterion, two independent engines caught it separately. The finding survived unchanged; only its basis got honest.

slides.h: Both engines passed the amended verdict — Track C is closed
b: The second pass came after repairing the one residue it named: the central finding was in the body but missing from the summary — the part people quote.
What remains open is not a gate but physics nobody has done: the optics of that wall.
